passage: In a school in Hamburg, Freya's turn came to read aloud, and she read with the soft accent of her home language. Somebody at the back mimicked it, and half the class laughed. Jana laughed too, then looked at her desk. At lunch the group table filled up without a space for Freya. She stood with her tray, heat rushing to her face, and decided that tomorrow she would speak more like them and say less about home. That afternoon the class teacher noticed the empty seat beside Freya, stayed behind after the bell and said, "I heard what happened. It is not your fault, and I will speak to the class tomorrow."

qa.q: What happened when Freya read aloud with the soft accent?
qa.a: Somebody at the back mimicked it, and half the class laughed.

qa.q: What is Freya feeling when standing with the tray and deciding to speak more like them?
qa.a: Freya feels ashamed and hurt, with anger mixed in, and a wish to hide part of home to be accepted.

qa.q: What turning point that afternoon helped Freya?
qa.a: The class teacher stayed behind, said it was not Freya's fault and promised to speak to the class the next day, which showed that an adult had noticed.

qa.q: What might Jana be feeling after laughing and then looking at the desk?
qa.a: Jana may feel guilty and uneasy, having joined the laughter without meaning harm and now unsure how to make it right.

grounding: A teenager is left out because of their language and accent, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide their identity.

passage: In the college canteen Avni, a scholarship student, put her steel tumbler on the table. "That is from the free-canteen scheme," someone said, and Sudha, the class rep, snorted. Half the table laughed. Avni's face went hot. She thought of telling them she had topped last term's maths, but it sounded like begging. Nobody asked her to the party planning. The next day she copied their way of talking in class and hid her old bag under the seat. On Friday the class mentor, Mr Menon, called her in and said, "I noticed the group leaving you out. That is not okay, and it is not about anything you did. I will raise it with the head today."

qa.q: What did Sudha do when someone mentioned the free-canteen scheme?
qa.a: Sudha, the class rep, snorted.

qa.q: What is Avni feeling when hiding the old bag under the seat and copying the group's way of talking?
qa.a: Avni feels ashamed and wants to blend in, with anger and hurt underneath; hiding the bag shows a wish to hide how different her life looks.

qa.q: What turning point on Friday helped Avni?
qa.a: Mr Menon called Avni in, said the exclusion was not okay and not about anything Avni did, and promised to raise it with the head that same day.

qa.q: How might Sudha, as class rep, see the moment at the canteen table?
qa.a: Sudha may have thought it was only a joke and wanted to fit in with the table, without seeing how it landed on Avni.

grounding: A teenager is left out because of their class background, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide their identity, until an adult acts the same day.

passage:
Avni, you asked why I never use my surname. Sit. This is your Mehak nani talking.
When I was fifteen, in our town, there was a girl called Sunanda who invited the whole class home for her birthday. I went, happy, with a hair clip wrapped in paper.
At lunch, all the girls ate inside on steel plates. I was given a leaf plate on the verandah. Sunanda's mother said something about our family, our caste, in a low voice. The other girls went quiet.
I ate a little and went home. I was angry, so angry, and ashamed, though I had done nothing.
For years after that I just wrote “Mehak” on forms. No surname. As if hiding it would make me welcome.

qa.q: What gift did young Mehak take?
qa.a: A hair clip wrapped in paper.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did young Mehak have after the lunch?
qa.a: She felt angry and ashamed at the same time, though she had done nothing wrong.

qa.q: What turning point in the story could have changed young Mehak's day?
qa.a: If one of the girls or an adult had spoken up or joined her on the verandah, she might not have felt so alone.

qa.q: How might the other girls have felt when they went quiet?
qa.a: They may have felt uncomfortable and unsure, knowing it was wrong but too afraid to speak.

grounding: An elder recalls being excluded at a teen friend's lunch because of her caste, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide her identity.

passage:
The school trip bus had broken down in the rain, and the teachers gave the boys ten minutes to choose roommates for the lodge before dark.
Hrithik stood holding his bag. His shoes, his cousin's old pair, had a sole flapping, and everyone had noticed that morning.
The boys paired off fast. “Anand, with me!” “Kunal, Rahul, you three!” Nobody said Hrithik's name. One boy looked at his shoes and whispered something. Two others laughed.
Anand glanced at him, then looked away.
Hrithik was put in the room with the teachers' extra bags. He lay on the bed, fists clenched, face hot. He hated them. He hated his shoes more. Tomorrow, he thought, he would wear socks over them and never mention his cousin again.

qa.q: Whose old shoes was Hrithik wearing?
qa.a: They were his cousin's old pair.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling as he lay on the bed?
qa.a: He felt angry and ashamed, hating the others and his shoes, and wanting to hide where they came from.

qa.q: How could the teachers have handled room choices better?
qa.a: They could have assigned rooms themselves so nobody was left out, especially under time pressure.

qa.q: Why might Anand have looked away?
qa.a: Anand may have felt guilty and uneasy but afraid to go against the group by picking Hrithik.

grounding: Shows a teenager left out on a school trip because of his family's poverty, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide it.

passage:
The birthday sleepover invitations went out in Class 9-B's group chat. Zeenat scrolled and scrolled. Everyone from her table was going. Her name wasn't there.
At lunch, Yogesh, who was hosting, said awkwardly, “It's just... my dadi is very particular. You know. About food and all. Because you're...” He trailed off.
The girls at the table stared at their tiffins.
Zeenat felt heat rise in her face. She wanted to shout. She also wanted to disappear. That evening, in front of the mirror, she practised saying her name as “Zee,” the way the girls in films did, and wondered if that would make things easier.
Her mother, passing the door, stopped and asked, “What's happened, beta?” Zeenat didn't answer at first. Then she told her everything.

qa.q: What name did Zeenat practise saying?
qa.a: She practised saying "Zee".

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when Yogesh trailed off?
qa.a: She felt angry and humiliated, wanting to shout and to disappear at the same time.

qa.q: What would help Zeenat most right now?
qa.a: Her mother listening calmly, telling her she has done nothing wrong, and perhaps speaking to the class teacher about the exclusion.

qa.q: How might the girls who stared at their tiffins feel?
qa.a: They may have felt awkward and a bit ashamed, knowing it was unfair but not sure how to speak up.

grounding: Shows a teenager excluded from a party because of her religion, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide her identity.

passage:
"Why aren't you coming to Kunal's sleepover? The whole group's going."
"Wasn't invited, Shreya."
"What? You sit with them every lunch."
"Arjun told me. Kunal's parents said 'not that one.' Because of my name. You know why."
"Rafiq, that's..."
"It's fine." He picked at his sandwich. "Maybe I'll just be Raf from now on. Nobody asks what Raf is."
"You'd change your name?"
"I'm so angry I could throw this tray. And then I feel stupid, like I'm the problem."
"You're not the problem. Come with me to Mrs Fernandes after lunch. Just so someone knows."
In the staffroom, Mrs Fernandes listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling me, Rafiq. This is not your fault, and your name is yours to keep. I'll speak to your class teacher today about how the group is treating you, and I'd like to call your parents this evening, if that's alright."

qa.q: What name does Rafiq say he might use from now on?
qa.a: Raf.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Rafiq describe?
qa.a: He feels angry enough to throw the tray and then ashamed, as if he were the problem.

qa.q: What did Mrs Fernandes's response get right?
qa.a: She thanked him, said it was not his fault, affirmed his name, and acted the same day with his class teacher and parents.

qa.q: How does Shreya see Rafiq's idea of changing his name?
qa.a: Shreya is shocked and upset; to her Rafiq is not the problem, so she brings him to a teacher right away.

grounding: Shows a teenager left out because of his religious identity, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide who he is to be accepted.
